vignette:
Priya is a 70-year-old South Asian woman, divorced, who works as a freelance photographer specializing in portrait and documentary work. She came to the clinic after decades of carrying what she described, in her first session, as "something I have never been able to put down." Her presenting concerns center on a history of severe physical abuse perpetrated by her mother throughout her childhood - abuse that was systematic, largely hidden from the outside world, and never, in any formal sense, addressed.

The abuse began when Priya was very young and continued through early adolescence. Her mother would strike her across the face and head, sometimes with an open hand, sometimes with whatever was nearby - a wooden spoon, a sandal, the edge of a book. What Priya remembers most vividly, when fragments do surface, is the particular quality of her mother's face in those moments: the expression that preceded the blow, the way the light in the room seemed to flatten and go still. She also remembers the sounds - a raised voice, the creak of a particular floorboard - and the way she learned to read these as signals. The abuse was never acknowledged by extended family, never named, and her mother lived into old age without any reckoning. She died several years ago. No one ever said it happened.

In the months and years following her mother's death, Priya noticed that something she had managed to keep at a distance was pressing closer. She found herself unable to deliberately reconstruct what had happened - when she tried to sit with the memories intentionally, they seemed to dissolve or slip sideways, leaving her with a residue of feeling rather than any coherent narrative. And yet, without warning, the terror would return whole: not as a memory she was observing but as something happening again, accompanied by the same physical dread she had felt as a child. She had come to believe that this was simply what she was - someone permanently marked, unable to trust her own mind.

The shame that accompanied any partial recall was, for Priya, among the most disorienting aspects of her experience. She had spent sixty years building a professional identity grounded in looking - in training her eye on other people's faces, in bearing witness. Yet when fragments of her own past surfaced, she felt an impulse to cover her own face with her hands, as though she herself needed to be hidden from view. This gesture appeared in sessions as well, her palms rising instinctively to her cheeks mid-sentence. She was certain, in those moments, that the shame belonged to her rather than to what had been done.

In her work, the consequences had become concrete. Portrait photography requires sustained eye contact, proximity, and the willingness to hold another person's gaze. Over the past two years, Priya had declined an increasing number of commissions, particularly those involving photographing older women. She would prepare, arrive, and then find herself managing an internal vigilance so consuming that the work suffered. She had come to believe she had to remain on guard at all times - reading faces for signs, anticipating shifts in mood - and this meant she was rarely fully present behind the lens. Colleagues had noticed. One long-standing client had stopped calling.

Outside of work, Priya described a life that had quietly contracted. She had been divorced for many years and had few close relationships. She had come to feel that she did not quite belong in any community - not fully Indian, not fully American, not part of a family in any recognizable sense. She spent a great deal of time trying to understand why her childhood had unfolded as it did, returning again and again to questions that had no satisfying answer. She tried hard to manage what she felt, keeping her voice even, her expression composed, not permitting herself to cry in sessions.

What finally brought her in was a conversation with a younger colleague who had begun therapy and spoken openly about it. Priya had driven home afterward and sat in her car for a long time. What she feared most, she said in her second session, was that it was too late - that at seventy, the damage was simply structural. What she hoped for, more quietly, was that someone might finally confirm that what had happened to her was real.
